title: SerDes Link Model
desc: A high-speed serial link modeled end to end in Python, then reimplemented in SystemVerilog and cosimulated against that model: a lossy channel, TX FFE, a CTLE, a 4-tap DFE, and a closed-loop bang-bang CDR that locks a 200 ppm frequency offset.

detail.body:
September 2026 · SerDes · Mixed-Signal · Personal Research

View the full project, code, and documentation: https://github.com/jackpham-rgb/serdes-link

Stage A writeup (Python model): https://github.com/jackpham-rgb/serdes-link/blob/main/docs/01-model.md

Stage C writeup (RTL): https://github.com/jackpham-rgb/serdes-link/blob/main/docs/03-rtl.md

[SECTION: What this is]

A link model for a 5 Gb/s NRZ serial link, built stage by stage in Python: a differential channel loaded from a Touchstone file, a PRBS15 transmitter with FFE and pulse shaping, a swept continuous-time linear equalizer, a 4-tap sign-sign LMS decision-feedback equalizer, and a closed-loop bang-bang (Alexander) clock-and-data-recovery loop that locks a 200 ppm transmit/receive frequency offset. The DFE, the CDR's digital loop filter, and a PRBS generator are then reimplemented in synthesizable SystemVerilog and cosimulated against the Python model using cocotb and Icarus Verilog, on the same vectors, not synthetic dummy patterns.

Currently running on a synthetic FR4 channel (scikit-rf); a real measured PCB channel is a planned follow-up stage, and drops in with no code changes since the channel loader just takes a file path.

[IMAGE: assets/img/serdes-closed_eye.png | The raw channel eye at 5 Gb/s over 12 inches of synthetic FR4 is fully closed]

[SECTION: Why I built this]

I wanted a from-scratch, first-principles view of the equalization chain that makes a multi-gigabit link work, rather than treating it as a black box: what a closed eye actually looks like, why a CTLE can overcorrect, what a DFE tap converging to a wrong sign looks like, and why a CDR loop that looks like it's doing something can still be unstable in a way that isn't obvious from a single plot. Reimplementing the digital control in RTL and proving it agrees with the Python model closes the loop between a model and something that could actually run on an FPGA or in silicon.

[SECTION: What I learned]

Six real bugs shaped this project as much as the working result did. In the Python model: a differential port-numbering convention that silently produced an all-zero transfer function instead of an error, a sign error in the DFE's LMS update that made a single tap diverge instead of converge, and a CDR feedback loop that looked functional but was actually positive feedback, confirmed only by deliberately sweeping the starting phase offset and watching it walk toward the wrong side. In the RTL: an inverted sign branch in the DFE tap update caught by hand before ever running a simulation, a cocotb race where reading a registered RTL output immediately after a clock edge can see the pre-update value, and a second, opposite-direction version of that same race that had been accidentally making a different test pass for the wrong reason. Every one of these was caught by a targeted test, not by inspection.

[SECTION: Results]

The raw channel eye at 5 Gb/s over 12 inches of synthetic FR4 is fully closed. CTLE peaking helps up to roughly 8-10 dB and then degrades the eye further past 15 dB, a real, measured over-peaking effect, not an assumption. The DFE's dominant tap converges to about -0.48 of the main cursor, and the post-DFE residual still shows four distinct levels rather than two, an honest uncancelled-ISI result rather than a decorative fully-opened eye. The CDR locks a 200 ppm offset with a phase-interpolator correction that ramps linearly to cancel it. On the RTL side: the PRBS generator matches the Python model bit-for-bit across 2000 bits, the DFE agrees on over 99% of decisions across 4000 samples, and the CDR's digital loop filter matches its fixed-point golden model exactly, cycle for cycle, on a real ~4000-step phase-detector sequence.

[IMAGE: assets/img/serdes-ctle_sweep.png | CTLE peaking helps up to roughly 8 to 10 dB, then over-peaking degrades the eye]

[IMAGE: assets/img/serdes-dfe_taps.png | DFE tap convergence (left) and the four residual levels left after equalization (right)]

[IMAGE: assets/img/serdes-jtol_and_lock.png | Jitter tolerance and CDR lock behavior]

[SECTION: Honesty line]

This is a link model plus a synthetic channel, not a measured board, plus digital control RTL cosimulated against that model, not something that has run on real silicon or an FPGA yet. Not a full-rate SerDes PHY tapeout. A measured channel (Stage B) and running this RTL on an FPGA (Stage 7) are planned next.
detail.status: Stage A (Python link model) and Stage C (SystemVerilog + cocotb) complete: channel model, TX, CTLE sweep, DFE, CDR lock, statistical BER, and a bit-exact RTL cosim of the DFE and CDR loop filter. Next: a measured PCB channel (Stage B).
